text:
The mistake is investing money before a liquidity buffer is held in an instant-access savings account. Without a buffer, a car repair, a back payment or a change of job can force you to sell units. The investment horizon is then determined by the next unexpected expense and no longer by your own plan.

The mistake is common because the buffer feels like giving up return. With an ECB deposit facility rate of 2.50% (valid from 16 September 2026) and a German inflation rate of 2.9% (August 2026), money in an instant-access savings account loses purchasing power in real terms. This is cited as an argument against the buffer, but it confuses purpose and return. The emergency fund is not an investment; it serves as protection against a forced sale at the worst possible time.

The cost arises in a drawdown, that is, a phase of heavy price losses. From 31 October 2007 to 9 March 2009, the MSCI World lost 57.46%. An investor who needed €6,000 during this period and had to sell units to raise it took the money from a portfolio that had lost just over half of its value. This part of their wealth no longer took part in the subsequent recovery. The paper loss thus became a permanent loss.
besser: First build up a buffer in an instant-access savings account that covers several months of fixed costs and foreseeable one-off expenses, and only invest the money above that. The buffer is judged by whether it prevents a forced sale. Its return is not a yardstick for this.

text:
The most expensive of all mistakes is selling after a sharp fall in prices. It is a reaction to the painful losses of the past, although this decision should be about the future performance of the portfolio. At the same time, it turns a temporary paper loss into a permanent real loss.

The mistake is common because people weight losses more heavily than gains. This loss aversion can be measured. The meta-analysis by Brown, Imai, Vieider and Camerer (2024, Journal of Economic Literature) combines 607 estimates from 150 studies. It arrives at a loss aversion coefficient of 1.955 with a 95% interval of 1.82 to 2.10. A loss is therefore felt roughly twice as strongly as a gain of the same size. In addition, there is action bias, which makes acting in a crisis feel more correct than doing nothing. Bar-Eli and colleagues (2007) found the same pattern in 286 penalty kicks they analysed, in which the goalkeepers almost always dived, although staying put would have been the best option.

What such a sale costs is shown by what happened next. The MSCI World has since more than made up for the slump of 57.46% and most recently gained 13.56% a year gross in the ten years to 31 August 2026. More generally, Morningstar's study Mind the Gap 2026 puts a figure on the cost of such moves into and out of the market. In the decade to 31 December 2025, the funds themselves returned 9.9% a year, whereas the average invested dollar earned only 8.7%. The gap of 1.2 percentage points a year arises solely from the timing and size of the buy and sell decisions.
besser: Before the crash, set down in writing what is to apply in a crash, and set up the savings plan so that it continues without a new decision. The rule has to be fixed before emotions set in, otherwise it will not be applied when it matters.

titel: Waiting for the right moment to invest
text:
The mistake is not investing available money until the market seems cheaper. Because nobody knows when that will be, waiting turns into being permanently uninvested. The supposed caution is then a bet against the long-term upward trend.

Many investors wait because buying shortly before a setback looks like an avoidable mistake in hindsight. Hindsight bias makes turning points seem recognisable in retrospect. They cannot be recognised in advance, because the best and the worst days on the stock market lie close together. Two of the three largest daily gains in the DAX fell on 13 and 28 October 2008, that is, in the middle of the financial crisis.

The cost can be calculated. An amount of US$10,000 that was invested continuously in the S&P 500 from the start of 1996 to the end of 2025 grew to around $192,167. Without the ten best days, the final wealth was 56% lower, and without the thirty best days around 84% lower. Around 76% of the best days fell in bear markets or in the first two months after them, that is, in the phases in which waiting seems most plausible.

There is also a counter-calculation. Conversely, if you had avoided the ten worst days of each decade since 1930, the result would have been much better than with continuous investment. It therefore does not follow from the data in general that timing is expensive. What does hold up is the statement that the best and worst days occur in the same phases of panic and cannot be separated from each other.
besser: Invest available money according to plan, either immediately or spread over a short period fixed in advance. The purchase dates follow the calendar and not the market situation.

titel: Mistaking individual shares for a diversified portfolio
text:
The mistake is equating many positions with diversification. Ten or twenty self-selected shares do reduce volatility compared with a single position, but they reduce the dispersion of the final result relative to the market only slowly. The portfolio continues to carry a risk for which there is no premium.

This follows from the core statement of the CAPM, according to which only systematic risk is rewarded. Unsystematic risk can be diversified away and therefore earns no risk premium. Investors who bear it anyway are not compensated for it.

William Bernstein simulated the effect with 98 randomly drawn portfolios of 15 S&P 500 shares each. In the period from December 1989 to November 1999, around 75% of them lagged behind the equally weighted market, which returned 24.15% a year. Individual portfolios were 5 to 10 percentage points a year below it. The reason is the right-skewed distribution of share returns. A few shares deliver most of the index return, and portfolios without these shares fall well behind.

In addition, there is survivorship bias in perception. Indices remove insolvent companies and add successful ones, which is why an index recovers. Individual shares do not necessarily recover, and entire markets sometimes do not recover for decades. The Japanese stock market took 34 years to regain its old peak.
besser: Build the core of the portfolio with a broad, globally diversified index and hold individual shares alongside it, if at all, only in a clearly limited proportion. How broadly a portfolio is diversified is shown by its coverage of the world market and not by the number of positions.

text:
Performance chasing means buying what has done well recently and selling what has done badly recently. The selection is based on performance that is already reflected in prices. As a result, buying in systematically falls in phases of high valuations and high attention.

The pattern is common because recency bias and social proof work in the same direction. A fund with three strong years appears to be a proven good fund, and the fact that others have already bought in is taken as confirmation. Asch's conformity experiments show how strong this mechanism is. In them, 74% of the participants gave an obviously wrong answer at least once, just because the group gave it. Without a group, the error rate was below 0.7%.

Morningstar measures the cost directly. In the decade to 31 December 2025, funds returned 9.9% a year, but their investors only 8.7%. The difference of 1.2 percentage points a year was due solely to timing and position size. The gap grows with volatility. In the calmest fifth of funds it was 0.4 percentage points, in the most volatile over 2.0, and for crypto ETFs between January 2024 and December 2025 around 14 percentage points a year. For broad US Large Blend funds it was zero, because hardly anyone moves in and out of them.

The Persistence Scorecard shows that good results in the past say nothing about future ones. Of the US equity funds that were in the top quartile of their category in 2021, none, except among small caps (around 2%), was again in the top quartile in each of the four following years up to 2025. By pure chance, the figure would have been 0.39%.
besser: Set the target allocation once and invest new money according to this split, regardless of recent performance. The fact that an investment has done best recently is the weakest reason to choose it.

text:
Home bias means weighting your own country much more heavily than its importance in the world market justifies. Such a portfolio feels familiar, and you feel well informed. However, it is a concentrated bet on a single economy, a single currency and a single industry structure.

In the MSCI World, the weight of the USA on 31 August 2026 was 72.14%, Japan accounted for 5.78, the United Kingdom for 3.53, Canada for 3.46 and France for 2.36%. Germany is not among the five largest countries and is below 2.4%. A portfolio of DAX constituents therefore covers only a small segment of the market. The effect is reinforced by familiarity bias, in which familiarity is mistaken for information.

The cost of concentration shows in the dispersion of results. The return triangle of the Deutsches Aktieninstitut covering 50 years shows for the DAX, with a holding period of 20 years, an average of 8.4% a year, 3.3 in the worst period and 15.2% in the best. Individual years came in at minus 43.9% (2002) and minus 40.4% (2008), others well above plus 30%. Investors who hold only one country bear this entire range without receiving an additional premium for it.
besser: Compare the portfolio with the weighting of the world market once a year and justify every deliberate deviation in writing. Anyone who wants to overweight the home market should be able to explain why they take on this additional risk even though it is not rewarded.

titel: Treating costs as a side issue
text:
The mistake is regarding ongoing charges as an insignificant decimal place. One percentage point a year sounds like little. Over decades, however, it has a multiplicative effect, and good years do not make up for it, because it is incurred in good and bad years alike.

Costs are underestimated because they are taken from the fund assets unnoticed, while the return fluctuates visibly. In The Arithmetic of Active Management (1991), William Sharpe describes the result as an arithmetic identity that holds without empirical data. Before costs, the average active return must equal the average passive return; after costs, it is necessarily lower. No study can refute this.

The EU securities regulator ESMA has measured the effect. Over the ten-year period from 2012 to 2021, active equity UCITS cost 1.50% a year, passive funds 0.53 and ETFs 0.31%. Net returns were 9.4% (active) compared with 10.6 (passive) and 10.4% (ETF) a year. The return gaps of 1.2 points (passive) and 1.0 points (ETF) are of the same order of magnitude as the cost gaps of 0.97 and 1.19 points.

In the following worked example, €10,000 is invested for 30 years at a gross return of 7%. With total costs of 0.20%, this results in €71,968; with 1.50%, only €49,840. The difference of €22,128 corresponds to around 31% of the final wealth and arises from 1.3 percentage points a year. Buffett cited the same relationship in his bet against the funds of hedge funds. The funds charged fixed fees of around 2.5% a year, which were incurred every year regardless of the investment result.
besser: Check the total expense ratio before every purchase. It is the only figure of an investment that is known with certainty in advance. If the products are otherwise the same, the price decides.

titel: Using an insurance policy as an investment
text:
The mistake is bundling risk protection and wealth building in one contract. This makes both more expensive and less flexible. The savings component also bears the sales and administration costs of the insurance wrapper, and a surrender always affects both parts.

Such contracts are widespread because they are actively sold, whereas you have to buy an index fund yourself. In addition, there is the status quo effect. Once a contract has been taken out, it keeps running because doing nothing is the most convenient option. Johnson and Goldstein (2003) show how strongly defaults work with an extreme example from another area. For organ donation, 12% consented in Germany with an opt-in rule, and 99.98% in Austria with an opt-out rule.

The costs have been quantified. For contracts from 2015 onwards, at most 2.5% of the total premiums may be zillmerised (Zillmerung), that is, offset straight away against the first premiums (maximum Zillmer rate under Section 4 DeckRV, the Actuarial Reserves Ordinance; previously 4%). The agreed acquisition and distribution costs can be higher and, for the surrender value of contracts from 2008 onwards, have to be spread over the first five years (Section 169 VVG, the Insurance Contract Act). This is why the surrender value in the first six years is usually below two thirds of the amounts paid in. For unit-linked insurance policies, a reduction in yield (Effektivkosten) of 1.8% to 2.7% a year is reported, and below 0.3% for a direct ETF savings plan. Classic contracts, for their part, yield little. The current rate of interest credited on endowment policies averaged 2.54% in 2026, with an inflation rate of 2.9% in August 2026. An Assekurata study of 30 life insurers found an average effective return on premiums of 0.14% for classic pension insurance policies in 2019, and for some providers it was negative.

The tax advantage of the policy is real, but smaller than the cost disadvantage. In a unit-linked policy, a 15% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) applies. Together with the taxation of only half the gain, which applies to payouts after a term of twelve years and after reaching the age of 62 (60 for contracts from 2005 to 2011; Section 20(1) no. 6 sentence 2 EStG, the Income Tax Act), effectively around 42.5% of the gain is taxable. This does not make up for a cost difference of around two percentage points a year.
besser: Separate risk and investment. Insure existential risks with pure risk policies and handle saving through your own securities account. Before signing any contract, ask for the stated reduction in yield and compare it with the costs of an ETF savings plan.

titel: Keeping the overdraft and investing at the same time
text:
The mistake is keeping expensive short-term debt while investing money at the same time. Taken together, this results in a position that pays a certain interest rate, known in advance, on the loan side and hopes for an uncertain return on the investment side.

The cause is mental accounting. In your head, the current account and the securities account are two separate pots; in your wealth, they are not. An investor who is €3,000 overdrawn and at the same time invests €3,000 in economic terms has a loan-financed investment, even if they have never called it that. The ECB main refinancing rate was 2.65% from 16 September 2026. Every unsecured consumer loan costs a significant premium over this rate, because no collateral has been provided.

The calculation compares a certain quantity with an uncertain one. Repayment yields a guaranteed, tax-free return equal to the loan interest rate. On the investment side, the DAX returned an average of 8.4% a year over 20-year holding periods, and 3.3% in the worst twenty-year period. Taxes still have to be deducted from this. If the gains are charged in full with 26.375% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) every year, a rough calculation leaves around 6% net on average. For an accumulating equity ETF with a 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung), whose tax falls due only on sale apart from the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale), it is just over 7% over 20 years. A loan interest rate above the respective after-tax return makes investing an expected loss compared with repaying. The loss is not certain, because the return on the investment fluctuates.
besser: Pay off consumer loans and the overdraft first, then invest. Treat the loan interest rate as a guaranteed return that an investment would first have to beat. The only exceptions are loans whose interest rate is below the expected after-tax return of the portfolio.

titel: Leaving everything in an instant-access savings account
text:
The mistake is confusing a stable nominal value with safety. In an instant-access savings account, the balance does not fluctuate. The purchasing power of this balance, on the other hand, does change, and only downwards.

The mistake persists because loss aversion is triggered by visible fluctuations and not by a creeping loss of purchasing power. A portfolio showing minus 20% is felt to be painful. An account that loses a little in real terms for three years is not. In Germany in 2025, around 14.1 million people owned shares, equity funds or ETFs, that is, about one in five people aged 14 and over. The majority still keep their money in nominal assets.

The cost can be calculated. With an inflation rate of 2.9% (August 2026), €10,000 without interest has a purchasing power of only around €7,510 after ten years. Just under €2,490 is therefore missing. The ECB deposit facility rate was 2.50% from 16 September 2026 and thus below the inflation rate. In addition, banks pass on changes in key interest rates with a delay and incompletely. By comparison, the DAX delivered an average of 8.4% a year over 20-year holding periods and still 3.3% in the worst period.
besser: Base the split between instant-access savings and investments on when the money will be needed and not on how you feel at the moment. Money for the next few years belongs in the account, money for the next few decades does not.

titel: Using the purchase price as the yardstick
text:
The disposition effect is the tendency to sell winners too early and hold on to losers too long. It is triggered by the purchase price as a reference point. Selling below this price would mean acknowledging the loss. Evaluation relative to a reference point, as described by prospect theory, leads investors to avoid this.

For the future performance of a share, the purchase price is irrelevant, because the price does not depend on what an individual investor paid. Nevertheless, it is the most widely used reference point among private investors. The most common expression of the mistake is the resolution not to sell until the position is back at zero. Moreover, the distinction between paper results and realised results is purely a mental effect. Paper losses are real losses and paper gains are real gains; they are separated only in mental accounting and in tax law.

Odean (1998) measured the effect in 10,000 securities accounts from 1987 to 1993. Winning positions were realised with a probability of 14.8%, losing positions with only 9.8%. Winners were therefore sold around 1.5 times as often. This is costly because the wrong positions were sold as a result. In the following twelve months, the winners sold achieved on average 3.4 percentage points more excess return than the losers held.

In December, the pattern reverses, because losses are then used for tax purposes. In that month, the rate of realised losses was 12.8% and that of realised gains 10.8%. Investors can therefore act rationally, but do not do so in the other eleven months of the year.
besser: Sell only according to rules set in advance, for example when a rebalancing range is exceeded, and never on the basis of whether the position is showing a gain or a loss. The only test is whether you would buy the position again today at this price.

titel: Buying more of losers to average down
text:
Averaging down is the active form of the disposition effect. Instead of merely holding the losing position, you increase it so that the average purchase price falls and a return to profit seems closer. The decision is therefore based entirely on a number from your own past.

Two cognitive biases work together here. Through the sunk cost effect, money already invested and research time already spent appear to be a reason to carry on. The gambler's fallacy supplies the justification that things are now due to even out. At the Monte Carlo Casino on 18 August 1913, black came up 26 times in a row, a streak with a probability of about 1 in 136.8 million. Players lost fortunes at the time because they bet on the supposedly overdue correction. The further price movement of a share, however, does not depend on the price at which you yourself bought it.

The costs arise at two levels. First, the expectation was wrong on average, because in Odean (1998) the losers held lagged behind the winners sold by 3.4 percentage points in the following year. Second, the cluster risk grows with every additional purchase, and a loss of 50% then requires a rise of 100% to get back to zero.
besser: Derive additional purchases solely from the target allocation and not from the purchase price. Before buying more, you should be able to explain why you would increase the position even if you were seeing it for the first time today.

text:
The mistake seems harmless, but it has consequences. Investors who check often also see losses more often, because over short periods, days with falling prices are almost as likely as days with rising prices. The combination of loss aversion and a short evaluation period is called myopic loss aversion. It leads to a degree of risk aversion that does not fit the actual investment period.

The design of the products reinforces the effect. Portfolio apps with push notifications, a display of daily performance and red colouring create artificially short evaluation periods. Frequent checking also leads to action bias, because anyone who has the figures in front of them all the time wants to do something. Benartzi and Thaler (1995) use this combination to explain the size of the equity risk premium.

The cost can be read from the account data that Barber and Odean (2000) analysed for 66,465 households from 1991 to 1996. The households that traded least often achieved 18.5% net a year, the most active fifth 11.4% and the market 17.9%. The difference of 7.1 percentage points a year between infrequent and frequent traders arose almost entirely from the cost of trading and not from poorer share selection.
besser: Switch off price-related notifications and set a fixed, infrequent date for looking at the portfolio, for example quarterly. Looking less often is an effective measure and not laziness.

titel: Buying based on star ratings and rankings
text:
The mistake is reading a ranking of the past as a forecast. Ratings and top lists order funds by their past performance. Whether the same order will also hold in future is rarely asked, although the question has been answered empirically.

Rankings are popular because they take a decision off your hands and because, following the representativeness heuristic, investors equate good past results with good management. In addition, there is survivorship bias. Elton, Gruber and Blake (1996) put the distortion caused by vanished funds at 0.9 percentage points a year, because closed and merged funds drop out of the statistics. Moreover, funds are merged into better sister funds without much fuss, so that their poor track record can no longer be found.

The findings on persistence are clear. Of the US equity funds in the top quartile in 2021, none in the overall group was again in the top quartile in each of the four following years up to 2025. By pure chance, the figure would have been 0.39%. Of 164 US large-cap funds that were in the top quartile in 2021, 20.1% were still there in 2022, and in 2023 the figure was 0.0%. Among mid-caps, too, no fund stayed in the top quartile over the full five years, and among small caps the figure was around 2%.
besser: Select funds by cost, index coverage and structure and not by stars or three-year returns. For every list of winners, check which funds are missing from it because they no longer exist.

titel: Trying to pick the successful active fund in advance
text:
The mistake lies in the assumption that good active managers can be identified in advance. That they exist is not disputed. Every year, some of the active funds beat their benchmark. However, the data show that they are few, that they keep changing and that the successful funds cannot be reliably picked beforehand.

The SPIVA scorecards measure this every six months and include closed and merged funds. As of 30 June 2025, 93.81% of all active US equity funds lagged behind the S&P Composite 1500 over 20 years, and 90.31% over 10 years. For investors in the euro area, the figures are even clearer. Over ten years, 98.22% of active global equity funds in euros and 97.21% of active US equity funds missed their benchmark; for German equity funds, the figure was 93.68%. Morningstar measures against index funds that can actually be invested in rather than against indices and arrives at success rates over ten years of 21% (June 2025) and around 25% (June 2026), and of 11.9% in Europe.

There is also counter-criticism. Cremers, Fulkerson and Riley (May 2026) show that the figures are milder if you weight by fund assets, assess closed funds on their return up to closure and compare with real index funds. Averaged over twelve categories of US equity funds, the underperformance rate over the 20 years to the end of 2024 then falls from 92% of funds to about 55% of fund assets. For bond funds over ten years, the picture is even reversed, with 37% instead of 71%. The study was funded by the association of active managers, but it can be recalculated. Even after this correction, fund selection for equities remains roughly a coin toss. Costs are already deducted in this, because the study compares net returns, so it does not show any advantage for active equity funds.

The only factor with stable predictive power is cost. Over ten years, 27% of the cheapest but only 15% of the most expensive active funds performed better than their passive counterpart. In US Large Blend, the figures were 15.4 versus 3.9%.
besser: Build the core of the portfolio passively and cheaply. Use active funds, if at all, only where success rates are higher and you consciously accept the costs. If you choose an active fund, choose the cheapest in its category.

text:
The mistake is treating year-end targets, price targets and economic forecasts as information from which an allocation can be derived. Forecasts are estimates and not measurements, and they are subject to overprecision. Confidence intervals are systematically set too narrow, and published point estimates seem more precise than they are.

Forecasts are used nonetheless, because a number makes it possible to act and because the anchoring effect works even with seemingly random numbers. Tversky and Kahneman (1974) spun a wheel of fortune in front of the participants that appeared to be random but was set to stop only at 10 or 65. With an anchor of 10, the participants estimated the share of African countries in the UN at a median of 25%, with an anchor of 65 at 45%. On the stock exchange, price targets, all-time highs and consensus estimates act as such anchors.

The track record is documented. Between 2018 and 2025, the consensus forecast of Wall Street strategists for the S&P 500 was within plus/minus 10 percentage points of the actual result in only one of eight years. The largest deviation came in 2022. The consensus was plus 3.9%, the actual result minus 19.4%, a deviation of 23.3 percentage points. In most of the past 16 years, the strategists underestimated the return, by around 10 percentage points on average.

Buffett's bet provides practical evidence. From 2008 to 2017, a simple S&P 500 index fund achieved a total gain of 125.8%, or 8.5% a year. Five funds of hedge funds, which together were invested in over 200 funds, achieved 0.3% to 6.5% a year. Taken together, they lagged behind in nine of the ten years.
besser: Read forecasts as entertainment and derive the allocation from your own investment horizon and risk-bearing capacity. If you formulate an expectation of your own, write it down as a range and evaluate it after twelve months.

text:
Overtrading is frequent reshuffling of the portfolio on the assumption that active intervention improves the result. The mistake lies less in share selection than in the cost of trading. Fees, bid-ask spreads and taxes on realised gains are certain to be incurred on every transaction, whereas the hoped-for improvement is not.

The cause is overconfidence in three forms: overestimation of personal ability, overprecision in forecasts and overplacement relative to others. Svenson (1981) found that 93% of the US students surveyed who held a driving licence placed themselves in the better half of their experimental group for driving skill. In addition, there is the illusion of control. Charts, indicators and trading interfaces create a feeling of controllability that is not justified for short-term price movements. Fenton-O'Creevy and colleagues (2003) studied traders at London investment banks. The traders most susceptible to the illusion of control were rated worse in analysis and risk management, contributed less to profits and earned less.

The figures are clear. In Barber and Odean (2000), the average household achieved 16.4% net a year while turning over 75% of its portfolio annually. The most active fifth achieved 11.4%, the market 17.9%. Before costs, frequent and infrequent traders hardly differed. Odean (1999) analysed 97,483 purchases and sales. The shares bought performed 3.31 percentage points worse in the following twelve months than those sold. The switch itself therefore reduced value even before fees and taxes were incurred.

The losses increase with trading frequency. In data from over 35,000 households, Barber and Odean (2001) found that men traded 45% more than women. Trading reduced men's net return by 2.65 percentage points a year and women's by 1.72 percentage points.
besser: Set a trading budget, for example at most four transactions a year outside the savings plan. Let every order sit for 24 hours and justify it in writing. Include doing nothing as an equally valid option in the checklist and record it as well.

titel: Cluster risk in your own employer
text:
The mistake is holding employee shares, share options or a large position in your own employer, although your employment income already depends entirely on this company. Job, portfolio and often also the property in the same location then together form a single risk.

The mistake arises from familiarity bias and from the fact that information about your own company is readily available. Your own company seems transparent, and your own judgement feels well founded. Familiarity, however, is not information. Discounts on employee shares do not offset a risk that materialises precisely when your salary is also at risk. In addition, sales are often postponed as long as the position shows a gain, and after that the disposition effect takes hold.

The cost is that of an unrewarded single-company risk. According to the CAPM, only systematic risk is rewarded. Single-company risk can be diversified away and therefore earns no premium. How large this risk is can be seen from Bernstein's simulation, in which 75% of the portfolios of 15 individual shares each lagged behind the market, and from the experience of entire sectors. Between 10 March 2000 and 9 October 2002, the Nasdaq Composite fell from 5,048.62 to around 1,114 points, that is, by 78%. An index recovers because insolvent companies are removed from it and replaced. With an individual company, there is no such replacement.
besser: Sell employer shares as planned once the holding periods have expired and transfer the proceeds into a broadly diversified portfolio. The rule is not to double in the portfolio the cluster risk that already exists through your own employment income.

text:
Without rebalancing, the portfolio's allocation shifts by itself. After several strong years for equities, the equity allocation is higher than planned, and the risk is greatest at the very moment when it seems smallest. After a crash, it is the other way round.

The omission is common because rebalancing runs counter to your own perception. It requires selling what has just done well and buying what has done badly. Recency bias and the status quo effect both work against it. This is why rebalancing only works if it is set up as a calendar entry or a fixed rule.

The effect has been measured. For a 50/50 portfolio of US shares and bonds from 1926 to 1994, Bernstein calculated a rebalancing premium of 0.49 percentage points a year. The benchmark is the weighted average of the two individual returns (7.85%); the return achieved with annual rebalancing was 8.34%. A portfolio that was never adjusted returned 9.17% over the same period, because its equity share rose sharply over time. The premium is not guaranteed. It arises from fluctuations and imperfect correlation and is reduced by transaction costs and taxes on realised gains. In any case, controlling risk is more important than the additional return.

There are researched rules for putting this into practice. Daryanani (2008) found a relative band of 20% around the target allocation to be advantageous. With a target allocation of 50%, the portfolio is therefore rebalanced at 40% or 60%. Narrower and wider bands performed worse, and a check every ten trading days was largely sufficient. Also common is Swedroe's 5/25 rule, with a band of 5 percentage points in absolute terms for large positions and 25% in relative terms for small ones.
besser: Choose a fixed rule, either an annual date or a band around the target allocation, and enter it in the calendar. In the accumulation phase, rebalance through new contributions where possible, because this avoids transaction costs and taxes.

text:
The mistake is treating the tax side as a formality. What is regularly overlooked is the exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag) that has not been issued and the tax on the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale), which is debited from the settlement account in January without any money having come in.

The mistake is common because the tax is withheld automatically and therefore goes unnoticed as long as you do not check. For 2021 and 2022, no advance lump sum arose because of negative base interest rates (Basiszins), which reinforced the impression that it did not exist. Since 2023, the base interest rate has been positive again; for 2026 it is 3.20%, the highest level since the investment tax reform was introduced.

The cost can be quantified precisely. The saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag) is €1,000 per person per year, or €2,000 for joint assessment. For tax deducted by the bank, however, it only takes effect if an exemption order has been issued; otherwise it can only be claimed via the tax return (Anlage KAP, the capital income annex). An investor who leaves it unused gives away up to €263.75 a year at 26.375% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer). For an equity ETF with a value of €10,000 at the start of the year, the advance lump sum for 2026 results in a base return (Basisertrag) of €224.00 (10,000 times 3.20% times 0.7). After the 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung), €156.80 remains, on which €41.36 of tax is due, payable in January 2027.

The bigger problem is liquidity. The bank debits the tax automatically, although no money has come in. If there are insufficient funds, it draws on a current account or instant-access savings account, asks for a deposit or reports the matter to the tax office. Some providers sell units in this case.
besser: Distribute exemption orders across all banks so that the allowance is fully used, and keep enough funds in the settlement account every January. Make a rough estimate of the advance lump sum once a year, because it can be calculated in advance from the base interest rate and the value at the start of the year.

text:
German tax law has only one genuine special pot. Losses from the sale of shares may only be offset against gains from the sale of shares (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG, the Income Tax Act). Everything else, that is, funds and ETFs, bonds, certificates, interest and dividends, goes through the general loss pot (allgemeiner Verlusttopf).

The mistake arises because the separation is not intuitive and most investors regard their portfolio as a single unit. Here, mental accounting exceptionally works the other way round. In your head, the portfolio is a single pot; in tax law, there are two, and losses can only be offset between them in one direction.

The cost hits the typical portfolio structure of an ETF savings plan plus a few individual shares. If an investor realises a loss of €5,000 from selling shares and a gain of €5,000 from selling ETFs, this is a zero-sum result economically, but not for tax purposes. After the 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung), €3,500 of the ETF gain remains taxable, on which €923.13 of flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) is due. The share loss remains unused and can only be offset against future gains on shares.

Conversely, losses on fund units end up in the general pot and can therefore also be offset against interest and dividends. The special pot restricts only the offsetting of losses from individual shares.
besser: Before every sale, check which loss pot the result falls into, and where possible bring share losses together with share gains in the same year. If you have several banks, request a loss certificate (Verlustbescheinigung) in good time. Otherwise, the loss can only be offset at the bank where it arose.

titel: Holding leveraged certificates as a long-term investment
text:
Knock-out certificates, turbos, mini futures and factor certificates are designed for short-term, monitored positions. The mistake is treating them like a leveraged index and leaving them in the portfolio because you believe in a particular direction of prices.

With a knock-out certificate, the barrier applies throughout the entire term and often also outside German trading hours. A brief price spike overnight is enough for a total loss, and a recovery the next day no longer helps. Moreover, the leverage is not constant. It rises automatically the closer the price gets to the barrier and is therefore highest in the phase with the greatest risk. Factor certificates do not track the underlying itself. They follow a strategy index that multiplies the daily percentage change by the factor. This makes them path-dependent, and they lose money in volatile sideways markets even if the underlying ends up unchanged.

In the extreme case, the cost is 100%, for two reasons that are independent of each other. The first is the knock-out itself, the second is issuer risk. Legally, certificates and warrants are bearer bonds (Inhaberschuldverschreibungen) and are not covered by deposit protection. If the issuer becomes insolvent, the investor faces a total loss, regardless of how the underlying has performed. The standard example is the collapse of Lehman in September 2008. In addition, there are the bid-ask spread, the premium (Aufgeld), financing costs and a management fee. As with funds, the issuer must state the costs in the key information document as total costs in euros and as a percentage.
besser: Do not use leveraged products for building wealth and, if at all, only with an amount whose complete loss has been planned for. Before every purchase, look up the strike price, barrier, ratio, financing costs and issuer.

text:
Contracts for difference (CFDs) are over-the-counter contracts with high leverage. The mistake is understanding the European protection rules as safety. They only limit the speed and the upper limit of the loss, not its probability.

Since the ESMA measures of 27 March 2018, fixed leverage limits have applied to retail clients: 30:1 for major currency pairs, 20:1 for non-major currencies, gold and major indices, 10:1 for other commodities and non-major indices, 5:1 for individual shares and 2:1 for cryptoassets. In addition, there is a margin close-out at 50% of the required minimum margin, negative balance protection per account and a standardised risk warning. In Germany, the obligation to make additional payments (Nachschusspflicht) has been ruled out since 2017.

Negative balance protection is often confused with safety. It only rules out losing more than the account balance. A total loss of the capital invested is explicitly possible and occurs very quickly with this much leverage. At 30:1, a price movement of just over 3% against the position is enough. The mandatory risk warnings of providers typically state that 70% to 85% of retail client accounts lose money.

Behind this lie the illusion of control and overconfidence. The trading interface conveys an impression of controllability, and frequent trading looks like diligence. Barber and Odean measured what this costs in the unleveraged case. The most active fifth achieved 11.4% net a year, the market 17.9%. Leverage multiplies this effect.
besser: Do not use CFDs for building wealth. The most important statistic on this is already in your own provider's mandatory risk warning.

text:
A backtest is a back-calculation and not experience. The mistake is reading such a curve as if someone had actually stuck with the strategy. During that period, however, neither the product nor the rule used for the back-calculation existed.

The mistake is common because backtests are systematically embellished from the moment they are created. If many variants of a rule are tested and only the best is published, the published result mainly reflects this selection. Huang, Song and Xiang show in The Smart Beta Mirage (JFQA 2023) that smart beta indices achieved an excess return of around 3% a year in backtests before the launch of the associated ETF, and minus 0.5 to minus 1% afterwards. According to their analysis, the cause is data mining in index construction and not capacity limits or timing. Chen and Velikov (JFQA 2022) recalculated 204 long-short anomalies, taking into account bid-ask spreads, the publication effect and modern trading technology. On average, 4 basis points a month remained, that is, around 0.5% a year.

The problem also affects reputable products and can be spotted in the factsheet. The Solactive index behind a well-known world portfolio starts at a base value of 1,000 on 31 July 2017, but has only been calculated live since 3 May 2023. All values before that are back-calculated. The return shown since inception is therefore based predominantly on a backtest.

The cost arises when investors buy in on the strength of the best back-calculation and are then disappointed by the actual performance. This is performance chasing with a scientific-sounding justification.
besser: In the factsheet, look for the live date first and count only the period after it as experience. Reduce every backtest return by transaction costs and taxes, and find out how many variants were tested before this particular one was published.

text:
The mistake is reading statistics without checking who is missing from them. Fund comparisons, strategy evaluations and success stories almost always contain only the survivors. This selection is not random, because it is precisely the failures that are missing.

The pattern has long been known. During the Second World War, Abraham Wald studied the bullet-hole patterns of returning bombers. He concluded that armour had to be added in the places where the returning aircraft showed no hits, because aircraft hit in those places had not come back. For funds, Elton, Gruber and Blake (1996) estimated the bias at 0.9 percentage points a year.

Of the active US equity funds that existed 20 years ago, only 37.29% still existed as of 30 June 2025. Over 15 years the figure was 50.90 and over 10 years 63.81%. In Europe, 58% of equity funds and 54% of bond funds survived over ten years. A comparison of the ten-year returns of all current funds in the USA therefore covers only just under two thirds of the funds. The rest, which consisted predominantly of the poor funds, is missing.

The same effect applies to indices and individual shares. Indices remove insolvent companies and add successful ones. An index therefore recovers more reliably than the shares it once comprised.
besser: For every success statistic, check who is missing, and look at fund comparisons only with survivorship-adjusted data, as used in the SPIVA methodology. A ranking without this correction is systematically embellished.

text:
The mistake is treating distributions as income that arises in addition to price gains. On the distribution date, the price falls by the amount distributed. The dividend is thus moved from the company's account to your own account and creates no additional value. Selecting by dividend yield is therefore selecting by distribution policy. This criterion says nothing about the quality of the companies.

Behind this lies mental accounting. Dividends are booked as income that you may spend, price gains as wealth that remains untouched. Two parts of the same total return thus become two pots with different rules. As a result, decisions turn out systematically different from those based on total return.

The contribution of dividends is undisputedly real and large. In the DAX, it amounted to around 2.78 percentage points a year between 1988 and 2025. This is the difference between the total return index (8.78% a year) and the price return index (6.00%). This argues for reinvesting dividends, but not for selecting by them.

In tax terms, the fixation costs money. Distributions are taxable immediately, for an equity fund at an effective 18.46% after the 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung), and have to be reinvested by hand. With accumulating funds, the tax is deferred, apart from the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale). In the accumulation phase, this is usually an advantage. In the withdrawal phase, on the other hand, a distribution can be practical.
besser: Select by total return and invest in accumulating funds during the accumulation phase. Regular payouts can be generated through planned sales of units. This is usually more favourable for tax purposes and independent of distribution policy.

text:
The mistake is deriving the size of a position from the strength of your own opinion instead of from the risk to your overall wealth. The more convinced someone is, the larger the position becomes. Yet it is precisely conviction that is systematically inflated by overconfidence.

Mathematically, losses have an asymmetric effect. A fall of 50% requires a subsequent rise of 100% to get back to zero. The Kelly criterion determines the position size that maximises long-term growth. Its most important result is that, when twice the Kelly fraction is staked, the long-term growth rate is zero in the usual approximation and becomes negative with an even higher stake. Beyond a certain point, a larger stake therefore leads to ruin.

Because the Kelly fraction is calculated from estimated probabilities and returns, and these estimates turn out too narrow when there is overprecision, practitioners usually work with a fraction of it. The cause of positions that are too large is well documented. Alpert and Raiffa as well as Lichtenstein and colleagues showed that confidence intervals are systematically set too narrow. Svenson (1981) found that 93% of the US students surveyed who held a driving licence placed themselves in the better half of their experimental group for driving skill.

The cost lies in the probability of dropping out of the market prematurely, and not in lost return. A portfolio that goes through a fall of 57.46% with three times the stake, like the MSCI World between October 2007 and March 2009, no longer exists afterwards.
besser: Determine the position size in advance as a fixed percentage of total wealth and choose the upper limit so that the total loss of a single position does not end the plan. Always formulate forecasts as a range and then double this range.

titel: Calculating the valuation towards the desired result
text:
The mistake is recalculating a valuation model with new assumptions until the calculated value is above the share price. The model then no longer serves as a check. It merely provides a justification for the desired result, and the spreadsheet becomes a tool of confirmation bias.

The terminal value in the DCF model is particularly susceptible. The denominator contains the expression cost of capital minus perpetual growth rate. As the growth rate approaches the cost of capital, the value therefore rises disproportionately. The KPMG cost of capital study 2025 reports an average WACC of 8.5% for companies from Germany, Austria and Switzerland, and by sector between 6.3% (Energy and Natural Resources) and 9.4% (Industrial Manufacturing, Technology). If you use a perpetual growth rate of 4% instead of 2% there, the denominator shrinks by almost a third, and the value of the company rises accordingly, without a single statement about the business having changed. Other typical calculation errors are assuming growth without the investment it requires, counting the tax shield twice, or forgetting net debt and mistaking the enterprise value for the equity value.

The cost can be seen in expensively valued quality companies of the past. The Nifty Fifty of the early 1970s were the best companies of their time and in 1972 traded on average at a price-to-earnings ratio of around 42, with individual shares considerably higher, while the long-term market average was 15 to 20. At the end of 1999, the Nasdaq Composite had a P/E ratio of around 200 and subsequently fell by 78%. A company's popularity is already reflected in its share price.

Graham formulated a counter-rule for this. According to it, the P/E ratio should be no more than 15, based on the average earnings of the last three years and not on the earnings of a single year.
besser: Instead of a point estimate, calculate a range across cost of capital, growth and margin, and also set up a reverse DCF that shows which assumptions the market is already pricing in. Fix the assumptions before looking at the share price.

titel: Mistaking the story for the analysis
text:
The mistake is treating a convincing narrative as evidence. A good story about a company, a technology or a market environment increases the willingness to buy, but not the probability of being right. It seems coherent because it is free of contradictions. Being free of contradictions, however, is no evidence that it is true.

Three mechanisms interlock here. Through the narrative fallacy, cause-and-effect relationships are constructed from random data. Confirmation bias means that afterwards only supporting information is sought. In 1960, Wason showed with his 2-4-6 task that people almost exclusively test confirming examples. The availability heuristic supplies the material, because what is easy to remember is considered likely. A survey by Franklin Templeton found that 66% of investors believed the S&P 500 had stayed flat or fallen in 2009, although it had risen by 26.5%. The respondents transferred their memory of 2008 to the year 2009.

In addition, there is social pressure. In Asch's experiments, 74% of the participants gave an obviously wrong answer at least once, just because the group gave it, while the error rate without a group was below 0.7%. If several of these effects act in the same direction at the same time, the result is what Charlie Munger called the Lollapalooza tendency. FOMO, the fear of missing out, is one such combination.

The cost is that of a procyclical entry, and it has been measured. Over the decade to the end of 2025, the difference between fund returns and investor returns was 1.2 percentage points a year. For particularly narrative-driven products it was considerably larger, for crypto ETFs between January 2024 and December 2025, for example, around 14 percentage points a year.
besser: Before buying, write down the three strongest counter-arguments and check which verifiable figure supports the story. Do not open a position without such a figure. Also, do not make an investment decision on a day on which you have consumed financial content on social media.
